blocks.text: Some tools just look things up. Others can change something or destroy something the moment they run.
Tool permissions are the rules that decide which tool calls happen right away and which ones need a person to say yes first.
This lesson covers how hosts judge risk, how approval works, and how allow lists and deny lists fit into the bigger MCP security picture.
1. Not All Tools Are Equally Risky

blocks.alt: Not All Tools Are Equally Risky
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586867-389892085.png
A tool that searches the web or reads a file is mostly harmless if the model calls it by mistake.
A tool that deletes a file, sends an email, or moves money is a completely different story.
The cost of a wrong guess is not the same for every tool, so the rules around calling them should not be the same either.

items: Low risk, reversible: searching the web, reading a document, checking the weather.
Medium risk, sometimes reversible: creating a draft, adding a calendar event, writing to a scratch file.
High risk, hard or impossible to undo: deleting a file, sending money, sending an email to a real customer, dropping a database table.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool type","Example","What happens if it runs by mistake"],"rows":[["Search or lookup","Search the web, read a file","Nothing bad, at worst some wasted time"],["Create or draft","Save a note, add a calendar event","Usually easy to delete or fix afterward"],["Destructive or irreversible","Delete a file, send a payment","Real damage that may not be undoable"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Read Only Tools vs Tools That Change Things

blocks.alt: Read Only Tools vs Tools That Change Things
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586867-269037872.png
A read only tool only looks at data, it never writes, deletes, or sends anything on your behalf.
A write tool changes state somewhere, in a file, a database, an inbox, or a bank account.
The read versus write split is the very first question worth asking about any tool before deciding how much trust it deserves.

blocks.title: A useful habit
blocks.content: Before you even look at a tool schema, ask one question. Does calling this tool only tell me something, or does it also do something. That single question sorts most tools into their right risk bucket.

blocks.text: 3. Why This Matters More With AI Agents
A human clicking buttons in an app usually understands what each button does before pressing it.
A model deciding which tool to call is guessing based on a prompt, and guesses are sometimes wrong.
When a wrong guess only means a wasted search, that is fine. When a wrong guess means a deleted file or a sent payment, that is not fine at all.

items: Models can misread an instruction and pick the wrong tool entirely.
Models can be tricked by content they read, a technique often called prompt injection.
A model has no gut feeling for consequences the way a careful human does, unless the host builds that caution in for it.

blocks.text: 4. The Idea of Approving a Tool Call
Approval means a tool call does not run the instant the model asks for it, it pauses first.
Someone or something checks the call, the tool name and the arguments, before letting it proceed.
That someone is usually the person using the assistant, and that pause is the single most important safety net in the whole system.
5. Host Level Permission Prompts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586867-378615890.png
The host is the application running the assistant, it sits between the model and every MCP server the model can reach.
Because the host controls that boundary, it is also the natural place to show a permission prompt before a risky call runs.
A good prompt tells you exactly what is about to happen, not a vague summary but the real tool name and the real arguments.

code.content:
Allow "send_email" to run with these arguments?

to: "customer@example.com"
subject: "Your order has shipped"
body: "Hi there, your order is on its way..."

[ Allow once ]   [ Always allow this tool ]   [ Deny ]

blocks.text: 6. What a Permission Prompt Actually Shows You
A weak prompt just says a tool wants to run, which tells you almost nothing useful.
A strong prompt breaks the call down into parts you can actually judge in a couple of seconds.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field shown","Why it matters"],"rows":[["Tool name","Tells you the category of action, read, write, or destructive"],["Arguments","Tells you exactly what target and what values are involved"],["Server name","Tells you which server, and therefore which codebase, is behind this tool"],["Risk hint","A short label like low risk or destructive, if the host bothers to show one"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Allow Lists for Specific Tools
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586867-418857730.png
An allow list names the exact tools that are permitted to run, everything else is blocked or needs a prompt.
This is the safer default for anything sensitive, since new or unexpected tools stay off until someone deliberately adds them.
8. Deny Lists and Blocking Dangerous Tools
A deny list works the opposite way, it names tools that are never allowed to run automatically, no matter what.
This fits well for tools everyone agrees are too dangerous to ever run without a human looking first.

blocks.title: Deny beats allow
blocks.content: If a tool somehow appears on both an allow list and a deny list, the deny list should win. Blocking a dangerous action is always the safer failure.

blocks.text: 9. Combining Allow Lists and Deny Lists
Real systems usually run both lists at once, an allow list for the common safe tools and a deny list as a hard backstop.
Anything not covered by either list falls into a middle ground, where the host asks the user directly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool status","What happens"],"rows":[["On the deny list","Blocked, no exceptions"],["On the allow list","Runs automatically, no prompt"],["On neither list","Host asks the user for a one time or repeated decision"]]}

blocks.text: 10. Always Allow vs Confirm Every Time

blocks.alt: Always Allow vs Confirm Every Time
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440586868-500106519.png
A trusted always allow tool runs the moment it is called, no prompt, no pause, because past decisions already covered it.
A tool that needs confirmation every time shows a prompt on every single call, even if the user approved the exact same call minutes ago.
The right choice depends entirely on how reversible the action is and how much it can hurt if the arguments happen to be wrong.

items: Always allow fits low risk, reversible, read only tools, since the downside of a mistake is tiny.
Confirm every time fits destructive or high value tools, since the downside of a mistake can be serious.
Some hosts offer a middle setting, allow for this session only, which resets back to asking the next time the assistant opens.

blocks.text: 11. Trust Levels and Scoping Permissions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440587200-966413034.png
Trust is not just a yes or no switch, it can have levels, and good permission systems let those levels show.
A tool might be trusted for reading your own notes but not trusted at all for touching a shared production database.

items: Scope by server, trust everything from a personal notes server more than an unfamiliar third party server.
Scope by tool, trust read_file but still confirm delete_file, even from the very same server.
Scope by target, trust writes to a scratch folder but still confirm writes to anything marked as production.

blocks.text: 12. Session Level vs Persistent Permissions
A session level permission only lasts for the current conversation, it resets the next time you start fresh.
A persistent permission is saved and remembered across sessions, so it keeps applying until someone changes it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Permission type","Lasts","Good fit for"],"rows":[["Session level","Until the current conversation ends","Trying out a new or unfamiliar tool"],["Persistent","Until manually changed","Tools you use constantly and fully trust"]]}

blocks.text: 13. Narrow Scoping Beats Broad Trust
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440587201-507796998.png
It is tempting to just always allow a tool entirely once it feels safe enough, but narrower rules are almost always better.
A narrow rule limits exactly what the tool can touch, instead of trusting it everywhere all at once.
14. How This Connects to the Broader MCP Security Model
MCP servers can come from anywhere, a coworker, a company you trust, or a stranger on the internet.
The protocol itself does not force a server to be safe, it only defines how tools are described and called.
Tool permissions are the piece that fills that gap, they let a host stay useful without blindly trusting whatever a server claims about itself.
15. Designing Tools With Permissions in Mind
If you build MCP servers yourself, naming and describing tools clearly makes permission decisions much easier for everyone downstream.
A tool called delete_file_permanently is far easier to judge correctly than one vaguely called manage_file.

items: Name destructive tools so the risk is obvious from the name alone.
Keep read and write actions in separate tools instead of one tool that quietly does both.
Document exactly what a tool changes, so a host or a user can write an accurate permission rule for it.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Say you connect an assistant to a server that offers search_docs, create_ticket, and delete_ticket.
search_docs is read only, so it sits on the allow list and runs without ever bothering you.
create_ticket and delete_ticket both change real data, so they stay on the confirm every time list, no matter how many times you have used them before.
Notice that the user, not the model, made the final call, which is exactly what a permission system is supposed to guarantee.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating every tool the same way instead of judging read only tools separately from destructive ones.
Marking a destructive tool as always allow just because prompts feel annoying.
Writing an allow list so broad it might as well not exist, such as allowing an entire server instead of specific tools.
Forgetting that a deny list should win over an allow list when the two ever disagree.
Assuming a tool name tells the whole story without checking what its arguments actually target.
Never revisiting persistent permissions, even after a tool starts being used for something riskier than before.

blocks.text: Practice
You are wiring up permissions for a server with three tools, get_weather, post_tweet, and refund_payment.
Decide which list each tool belongs on, allow, confirm every time, or deny, and write a short permission config for it.
Key Takeaway
Tool permissions turn a model guess into a checked decision, using allow lists, deny lists, and prompts so risky calls never run unnoticed.
